[h1]"Desperation can bring out the demon in the best of men"[/h1]

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Ghost of Tsushima is an open-world adventure game set in 13th-century feudal Japan and seeks to deliver a gripping tale of one man's struggle to face the demons who have invaded his home and the demons that struggle within. But does it have what it takes to repel the invasion, or is it destined to be crushed against the tide?

[table]
[tr]
 [th][b]🟩 Positives[/b][/th]
 [th][b]🟥 Negatives[/b][/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
 [td]🟩 A truly captivating original story that blends historical accuracy with compelling fiction with seamless authenticity.

🟩 Fast, flowing, and well-thought-out combat makes every encounter feel like a challenging experience, especially on Lethal difficulty, which makes all attacks fatal on both sides of combat.

🟩 A robust world filled to the brim with activities, unique encounters, loads of options for dealing with different situations and an arsenal of armour and tools to match.

🟩 A visually stunning open world that is breathtaking to adventure through is made only better by the extraordinarily well-designed photo mode that allows you to unlock your creativity with sizeable customisation options.

🟩  The audio quality is not as substantial as the visual, but it still provides an impressive attempt at immersion on all fronts. The soundtrack has been designed to captivate your emotions throughout the campaign, and both the English and Japanese voice-acting cast are perfect choices for the main characters, which is somewhat of a rarity.[/td]
 [td]🟥 The AI is not particularly smart or challenging and is particularly easy to funnel into kill zones even on the highest difficulties

🟥 Enemy variety is not enormous, and by the time you reach the end of the second act, you will have encountered everything the game has to throw at you.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
It is late into the 13th century in feudal Japan. The Mongol empire has already laid waste to countless nations in their campaign to conquer the East. In their invasion, they eventually land on the shores of Tsushima, and the brave samurai rise to fend off the massing hordes. Jin Sakai, the main character, is amongst their number and watches as the samurai defences fail and the invading forces claim a foothold in his homeland.

It is here as the last of his clan, where Jin must rise against the invaders, cast aside his honour and do what he must to protect his home and the people.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3250555309

But will his quest for vengeance and urge to do what must be done allow his demons to consume him?

Ghost of Tsushima is a well-written and paced plot that delivers substantial emotional investment in Jin’s story, and the fate of the entire island. This is done by tailored questlines, side stories and considerable quantities of collectibles that provide insight into the state of the world and what has led to the current situation. There are some moments where you feel the story might have dragged on a little, but these are quickly dissipated as each act hits its climax and can be easily avoided by not spending too long trying to 100% each zone before moving on with the story.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[h3]”But we are all killers”[/h3]
This game revolves heavily around combat, which can take many forms throughout the campaign.

A majority of the game will take place in open combat, where you are fighting against large groups or waves of enemies in swordplay. Sword fighting is pretty simplistic as you only have very few abilities at the beginning of the game. Over time it does grow in complexity if you wish to master the many facets of it, such as stance dancing to attack enemies of different proficiencies or deflecting the enemy advances to deliver crushing counterattacks to thin their numbers.

There are more ways to fight, whether you choose a stealthier approach and use long grass to mask your entry into a base and take them all out before they know you’re there, or you use a bow to pick enemies off from range there are tools and skills to benefit the way you want to play and build your character to optimise them.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3250556642

Levelling Jin is done in a standard way where killing enemies and completing activities like side quests will net you experience points which can then be invested into a moderately sized series of skill trees.

While the general story is linear, how you approach missions isn’t linear, allowing you some flexibility in dealing with different situations and giving you real control over how things turn out in each encounter.

[h3]”The strength we need is all around us”[/h3]
Exploration plays a monumental role in Ghost of Tsushima as it's the only way to experience everything the game has to offer, is to explore the sprawling world around you, following clues to points of interest, and completing the activities there.

Activities in the open world, such as bamboo strikes and meditating in hot springs can grant you substantial boons to your combat and survivability, so it’s worth exploring to find them all.

The map does play a part in this and can help you in navigating the world allowing you to set waypoints to make your traversal easier, it is not a flawless system and it takes some getting used to before you can use it to its full capability.

[h3]The path of a legend.[/h3]
The game also has quite a substantial multiplayer mode that allows for coop play to complete missions that earn experience points and gear for your characters so you can level them up and equip them for the battles ahead. I had quite a lot of fun with this game mode and wished it was a full game on its own as it's quite an enamouring experience filled with content and interesting stories. Maybe one day!

[h1]Audio and Visual[/h1]
Ghost of Tsushima provides a breathtaking visual experience that only broadens as you explore its robust and flowing world. With a well-designed photo mode to capture the moments as you run, jump and climb across its expansive wilderness.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3250558169

The audio is of exceptional quality as well but lacks a little variety at times. This isn't a massive qualm as the game is large and you don't spend much time listening to the nature around you or the soundtrack.

[h1]PC Performance and Specifications[/h1]
With the game on Ultra settings at 2560 x 1440, it ran impeccably smooth, especially considering it's a PlayStation port. Sat at a firm 60 FPS the entire time and never really deviated from that.
RAM: 32GB 3200GHz G-Skill (DDR4)

[h1]Final Thoughts - Very Good[/h1]
[url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2529084785]Review chart here.[/url]
Ghost of Tsushima is a well-thought-out and passionately designed experience that doesn't deviate from its goals of immersion and substance. Providing a compelling storyline with interesting characters and an enormous open world to explore you will have your hands full for a lot of hours as you bring peace to the wartorn lands of Tsushima.

In all of my many years of playing Videogames, across many platforms, over 10,000+ hours of playtime total I haven’t come across many masterpieces.

However, Ghost of Tsushima is more than a masterpiece. It’s is ART.

The combat system in Ghost of Tsushima has got to be the smoothest of any game I have ever played. No hiccups, no jittery movements. Every button and action used smoothly transitions from one to the next and honestly it’s just amazing. 

The game direction is the best I have ever seen. No stupid marker on the screen in your face. No UI for the most part of travelling. The game uses the wind to guide you through Tsushima and Iki Island. It adds a level of immersion I hadn’t ever thought possible in a game.

The game itself is beautiful. Everywhere you go in this game and in any weather looks fantastic that a screenshot from anywhere anytime can look like PURE CINEMA. The trees, the grass, the sun as it sheds its light on everything just looks… wow!

Throughout my gameplay of this game I have encountered only two bugs. On Iki island there was a rock and you could see a few pixel gap where you could see through the world. But honestly it is super easy to miss. The other was a fault of my personal settings so I won’t include it.

The story is one that hits home for me. Balancing what is right and what is not and of one’s own honour. It is amazing. Literally goosebumps whenever I play or watch the game. I bought Ghost of Tsushima in a real tough time in my life and had no spoilers and thus NO REGRETS.

The music is on another level. I’ve never really stepped into the Japanese genre of music before and this game has it dialled up to 100x. The music gives goosebumps every time, it matches the feel and the action the game is going for at every turn. It is hard to put into words how good it is. How AMAZING it is!

Japanese culture is somewhat inaccurate as the whole Honour theme wasn’t prevalent until 200 years after the Mongolians attempted to invade the mainland after conquering Tsushima and Iki. But their faith, their traditions, the way the armour looks and how many times you hit an enemy with your katana to kill them is really realistic. As blades back then were too thin to cause real damage.

This has changed my opinion on games and is officially my favourite game of All Time!
I wholly Recommend You Buy It!

Ghost of Tsushima is one of those games that will definitely make you feel cooler than you actually are. Just a moment ago you might have been fumbling and tripping in real life, but now you are Jin Sakai, cutting down Mongols like it’s nothing, as if you've been training with a bamboo sword under a waterfall your whole life. The game is stunning, cinematic, and almost a spiritual experience... unless you take into consideration the fact that you stop during a fight to pet a fox. 

The Director’s Cut is essentially the same game, but with an amplified effect of everything, more island, more narrative, more wind dramatically blowing through your cape as you contemplate honor and trauma. The Iki Island expansion is Jin’s journey in therapy, which is cleverly disguised as a side quest. It is aesthetically pleasing and tragic at the same time, and sometimes it can be the “my dad didn’t hug me enough” energy. 

The visuals are worth discussing. This game doesn’t have graphics, it has art. Every single frame could be a piece of art that people museum it and they silently say “wow, the composition.” You might find yourself in the middle of a fight and suddenly stopping to take pictures because the sunset is just too beautiful. While you’re technically supposed to be saving Japan, you are here instead, like a feudal times influencer, adjusting filters and focal depth. 

The fight? Exquisitely sharp. It’s a combination of ballet and murder. Each stunt and every sword strike is real and believable. You’ll transition from button, mashing panic to perfect timely parry that will make you say “yes” quietly to yourself at 2 a.m. They even have a standoff mode where you can basically act as the main character of every cool samurai movie you’ve ever seen, with the difference that you are the one who doesn’t fail and misses. 

Also, the dual, audio Japanese voice acting? The best. If you opt to play in English, that’s ok but playing in Japanese and with Kurosawa mode on is an absolute vibe. Black and white, film grain, wind that is blowing dramaticaly, it really gives you the feeling that you are watching a masterpiece from the 1950s, except without the smell of the film burning. 

The Director’s Cut is not a major overhaul of the game, but a kind of a mirror polish. Emotionally, the weight comes from Iki Island and a handful of new gadgets, and on PS5, ‘blink and it’s done’ would be a pretty accurate description of the load times. It’s essentially the same game, only smoother, prettier, and slightly sadder in a good way. 

Essentially, Ghost of Tsushima: Director’s Cut is the result of art, combat and open, world design teaming up to form a boy band. It’s gorgeous, emotional, and at times, silly, in the way that only a game that lets you write haikus about death next to a waterfall can be. 

Play it. Then play it again. And don’t forget to pet every single fox, they really deserve it.

I didn't really have expectations going into GoT, and for the first few hours it didn't blow me away. When the story properly kicks off, it is very good from a few hours in to the end. They deal with open world quest objectives in a creative way where the direction the wind blows in is the direction you're meant to go in. It's not in your face, it's not a compass with a big yellow arrow on it that says "GO HERE". All direction you're given feels more like guidance than telling you what to do. 

It does suffer from the common problem in action games where the combat can feel shallow in the beginning, but as you get a grip of the mechanics and unlock more "abilities" you can mix up each fight massively. You switch between stances in a way that's not clunky, you have batman-like gadgets as well as your sword and bow, everything feels so fluid and smooth to use. When you get the ability that lets you use slow-mo when aiming your bow it becomes even more fluid where you can headshot multiple people from a few feet away in under a second the instantly throw down a smoke bomb and assassinate another two - it's more thrilling than I'm giving it credit for and that's just one of many "techniques" you can use. Ghost of Tsushima is what assassins creed has been trying to be, but Ghost does a far better job since the AC quests are quests where you tick a box by gathering an item or clearing out this camp of bandits or deliver this thing to this person - Ghost has absolutely none of the tedium. There are bandit (mongol) camps to clear out in quests but you're not doing it to retrieve an item, there is always a story justification or a character you're helping with a longer quest so it feels like it has purpose. 

What makes this special is the conflict between honor and pragmatism, a common thread all the way throughout. I loved the second 2/3 of the story, but the first 1/3 does feel slow as there's a lot of travelling around meeting new characters and learning their stories. They're all very cool but traversal in the first chapter I felt was more tedious than the second two. I still enjoyed it a lot but felt that the first chapter is the weakest. Each character has it's own set of story quests to follow where you help them avenge someone or hunt someone down or something like that. 

The main antagonist is the leader of the mongol invasion, and his soldiers. The music is a cool mix of Mongolian throat singing and the type of music you'd expect in a Samurai game. It's a cool blend of cultures since the Mongols have already taken over certain areas and you get to see their culture next to the Japanese. I liked the enemy variety as well, the way that you deal with each enemy type keeps encounters fresh. 

The DLC has a very cool story where you confront something which is mentioned in the main game several times, it fits into the base game very seamlessly and there is a good amount of content on the new island. 

Overall it's a nice breath of fresh air in a world of open world RPGs - it has some RPG elements but you're not levelling up and distributing your points. It's first and foremost an action game, and I think it deserves it's reputation as one of the best.

Ghost of Tsushima is an open world third person action game, set in the age of samurai. When the Mongol empire invades Tsushima island, player character Jin Sakai must fight to defend his home, and defeat the Mongol army before they can attack the Japanese mainland.

[h1]Gameplay (high quality)[/h1]

•	Combat system feels similar to Batman Arkham and Shadow of Mordor, where you’ll need to closely watch enemy attack animations to correctly time your dodges and parries, before performing your own counter attacks.

•	The best games give the player many tools to choose from when developing your own playing style. While Jin primarily fights with a katana, and can switch between stances which are more effective against different enemy weapon types, he can also attack from range using a bow, throwable daggers and bombs, and poison darts. 

•	Another tactic which the player can take advantage of is to perform stealth kills on unaware enemies from behind or above, like a ninja. This is a useful way to reduce the number of enemies before a fight begins. There are a couple of missions where stealth is enforced, and being seen will result in an instant failure, but most of the time this isn’t a problem.

•	You can heal at any time by spending resolve earned from killing enemies.  This means that most fights feel comfortable on normal difficulty, even when significantly outnumbered, especially later in the game after upgrading weapons and armour, performing tasks in the open world to increase maximum health and resolve, and with charms equipped to further increase attack power, reduce damage taken, and generate more resolve.

•	Enemies include Mongol soldiers and Japanese bandits, equipped with sword, shield, spear, or bow. Some enemies can use flaming sword and arrow attacks, and the Iki island expansion introduces shamans who can buff the attack power of their allies. You’ll also be attacked by aggressive wildlife including, dogs, bears, and wild boar.

•	Archers don’t pose much threat because they literally shout “get down” before they fire (even when there’s no ally in their firing line), so you always know when to duck. The only time an archer will hit you is when you don’t know they’re there because you’re concentrating on fighting someone else.

•	Sometimes enemies will get scared and run away when you perform a special move, which feels realistic.

•	Boss fight duels can be annoying because the combat mechanics are different to regular fights. The way Jin moves feels strange, like you’re tied to the boss by an invisible rope, meanwhile their multiple hit attack combos are often too fast to consistently block/dodge. Especially later in the game, I won these fights by exploiting a charm which constantly regenerates resolve to essentially give myself infinite health.

•	In addition to the main quest, open world activities include side quests, companion quests, outposts to liberate from Mongol control, and various collectables to find.

[h1]Story (high quality)[/h1]

•	Story is well written and features several interesting characters. Gathering allies and attacking large castles feels like you’re part of a big war. There’s a strong focus on the samurai code of honour, and whether Jin’s evolving tactics can be justified.

•	Side quests feature unique stories where you’ll need to defend civilians, assist companions with their problems, and investigate ghost stories.

•	Voice acting is excellent.

[h1]Technical (high quality)[/h1]

•	It took me 55 hours to complete the main story, expansion, and most side quests.

•	Environment looks stunning, with farms, villages, temples and castles surrounded by forests, rivers, and fields of colourful flowers.

•	Controls are fully rebindable and work great with mouse and keyboard.

•	I didn’t notice any bugs or crashes, and my framerate was mostly stable with most settings on high or maxed at 1440p (RTX 3080, i7-12700K, 32GB DDR4).

•	However, I did see some stuttering after lengthy playing sessions. There’s some mention on the forum of a memory leak which seems consistent with what I experienced. I usually played between 90-120 minutes at a time without a problem. A couple of times I went over 2 hours and I started to see some stuttering. Performance during the Iki island expansion seems worse, where stuttering starts after around 1 hour.

[h1]Recommendation[/h1]

Ghost of Tsushima is an excellent game which I highly recommend to all players because both the combat and story are very enjoyable. There’s enough content to justify buying at any price.

Hopefully Sony bring Ghost of Yotei (and their other exclusives) to PC quicker. A few months delay is fine, but don’t make us wait years.

There’s no other game quite like Ghost of Tsushima, it had me hooked from start to end. Might be the most atmospheric game I’ve ever played, the visuals and music are gorgeous, it’s so immersive. The HUD is very limited, no mini-map just a subtle guidance system and it’s all the better for it, the game begs you to explore the beautiful island and find its secrets and I was happy to oblige.

The main story is only half the enjoyment here as the side content is fairly extensive, I got close to 100 hours of playtime which is more than I expected and I enjoyed every minute of it. Each side story got me more invested in the characters so each beat of the main story was that much more impactful.

But it’s not just the story, characters and world that are intriguing, the main draw of this game for me was the combat. Quite possibly the best combat system in a game ever maybe besides Sifu which is definitely saying something. As you progress it gets more challenging but as you unlock new stances, equipment and charms it also gets so much more rewarding and it’s smooth af, from rushing in and slaughtering mongols as a samurai, to sneaking around with a more ninja like approach and cutting their throats, the deliciously violent gameplay is so satisfying.

This director’s cut also includes the Iki Island expansion which as the name suggests adds a whole new island and brand new story arc which is best played after liberating Tsushima imo. A masterpiece of an expansion and a masterpiece of a game. There’s also a separate co-op mode which I haven’t played much of but seems fun. 

Overall though this has definitely become one of my favorite games of all time.

Ghost of Tsushima is pretty much everything I want in a game.

A beautifully detailed and immersive world, a memorable protagonist, interesting and complex characters, great voice acting, a perfect soundtrack that blends in seamlessly whether you are in an epic battle or just taking in the sights near the cliffs, excellent and responsive gameplay, gear upgrades, tons of things to find and discover, and an incredible, emotional story.

Every inch of Tsushima felt screenshot worthy. I constantly found myself stopping just to take in the scenery, and it was ridiculously easy to get lost in this gorgeously colorful world while cutting down Mongol invaders.

The major story missions are just fantastic. They are packed with story, character moments, and excitement, all building toward an emotionally impactful final duel that, when it was over, left me sitting there for a minute thinking, "Man."

This was a "Man" game for sure.

The DLC only made it better by adding even more story that fills in Jin's past, his upbringing, and how he ultimately processes the man he chose to become for Tsushima. It was a great addition to an already great story.

I completed everything in the base game and the DLC, then went back for a New Game+ playthrough. Normally, a NG+ achievement annoys me, but I was actually happy to play through the main story again. I went into NG+ thinking it would be even more fun to experience the main story without having to worry about all the side missions and exploring every inch of the island looking for sword kits, charms, flowers, shrines, fox dens, and healing pools.

I was very wrong.

I found myself wanting to replay every mission in the game. I didn't, but I honestly felt like my second playthrough was less special because I skipped all of those side missions. Those little stories and all of the stuff you stumble across while exploring are such a big part of what makes this game special.

Then there is Legends.

I have to admit, I went into Legends with annoyance and skepticism. Another multiplayer achievement. Great.

At first, Legends just felt off to me. It was darker, I had no idea what I was doing, and I struggled badly playing through the story solo. By the time I reached Ki 32, I finally decided to figure out what I actually needed to do to get better.

A few days later, I was comfortable enough to turn Matchmaking On.

100 hours later, I'm hooked.

I begrudgingly came for the achievements, but stayed for the gameplay, story, gear grind, and fun. I never expected Legends to become something I would actually spend that much time playing, but here we are. It's also pretty remarkable that this entire multiplayer mode is free.

And even in 2026, there is still no shortage of people playing. I've rarely had to wait longer than a minute to get into a matchmaking story or survival run.

Ghost of Tsushima is one of those games where I kept finding reasons to play just a little longer. Finish one more mission. Find one more shrine. Upgrade one more piece of gear. Try one more Legends run.

Then suddenly I'm over 100 hours in.

The funny thing is, I started this game expecting to love the single-player experience and tolerate the multiplayer long enough to get the achievements. Instead, I ended up loving both.

Great world. Great characters. Great story. Great gameplay. Great DLC. And somehow, a multiplayer mode that I didn't even want to play became another 100 hours of fun.

Yeah.

"Man."

I will break down everything in a Pro's vs Con's list.

[h1]Pro's[/h1]
+ Story. If you ever wanted a masterclass in storytelling, Ghosts of Tsushima has one of the best story's I've ever had the privilege of playing. From the main story, the DLC's & every little side quest, mostly everything in this game is executed to perfection. Don't be surprised if you get attached to several characters.
+ World. Has a wide variety of beautiful landscapes to enjoy & get lost in. Honestly, sometimes I forgot I had a war to fight. [i]Yes, there's a Photo Mode if you're interested in that. [/i]
+ Combat. Once you've progressed a little with the story, gotten used to how the combat system works & learned some additional stances, the combat can be very fluid. From Samurai-standoffs, a sneaky ninja approach, or a merging of the both. You won't feel locked to just one approach. [i](You can even participate in a few duels throughout the game).[/i]
+ It's graphically impressive, if you have a decent PC. I've added my specs to this review.

[h1]Con's[/h1]
- Bugs. There's a couple of bugged achievements. One I gained without doing the prerequisite task (Grand Opening), the other (Common Courtesy) which is a DLC achievement, didn't pop until I returned to one of 5 areas, even though I had completed all of the related tasks. Other than that, nothing of note with bugs.
- Multiplayer. While I don't find it to be completely bad, it's just... Meh. Frankly I find it quite boring in comparison to the rest of the game.
- PSN Account Requirement. 

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
Without a doubt, Ghosts is one of the best experiences that you could you ever treat yourself too. I bought it on sale, which I usually recommend everyone do in today's economy, however you wouldn't be disappointed if you bought it at full price as it's undoubtedly worth every penny.

[h1]A Different Take of Assassin's Creed[/h1]

Before we get to the Assassin's Creed part, let's start with the obvious. The visuals in Ghost of Tsushima are stunning. The landscapes are beautifully crafted and are very versatile. There are many distinct and gorgeous biomes.  The changing weather and time of day add to the immersive experience. The attention to detail in the environment, from the swaying grass to the falling leaves and particles, all take Ghost of Tsushima to another level visually.

The other best thing about Ghost of Tsushima is the combat, especially the animations. While the animations during combat are excellent and add realism to every move, the combat itself can become repetitive. For 90% of the fights, you can defeat the enemy by doing this combo. Change Stance according to the enemy, Triangle ⮕ Triangle ⮕ Square ⮕ Square. That's it, that's how you kill every enemy in Ghost of Tsushima, which makes an extremely easy game brainlessly simple and extremely repetitive combat-wise. Even with the different stances and special moves, the core combat loop doesn't change much throughout the game. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3257271909

While the theme of Mongolians invading your country and you as the main character saving your country is promising and exciting, the way this concept is presented to you is very boring. Most of the cutscenes are two characters standing and talking to each other like they had a stroke with no emotion. And most cutscenes are lengthy and lack dynamism, making them feel like a chore to sit through. They are no different at side missions or open-world activities, which make them feel like fillers. The repetitive nature of the dialogue and the predictable structure of the missions contribute to this sense of monotony. These detract from the overall impact of the story. I found the scenario very predictable, the villain extremely generic, and the characters very uninteresting overall.

The worst thing about Ghost of Tsushima is the open-world design. The game’s structure is heavily inspired by Ubisoft’s open-world formula seen in games like Assassin's Creed and Far Cry. The missions and activities often become repetitive. Many side quests follow a similar structure: go to a location, defeat enemies, and return. If not, you track footsteps, examine items, or rescue hostages for minutes that lose its charm real quick when you are doing the same thing for the 20th time. These activities lack variety and creativity, making the exploration feel like a checklist rather than an adventure. The world, though stunning, lacks the interactivity and dynamic events found in other open-world games like The Witcher 3 or Red Dead Redemption 2, making the world of Tsushima feel soulless.

The AI is another thing where this game is very similar to Assassin's Creed. The AI is disappointingly bad and often behaves in ways that break immersion. The "detection bar" famous in Ubisoft titles, is present in Ghost of Tsushima. Enemies won't notice you if you quickly kill someone in their line of sight just because the detection bar hasn't filled yet. The music is not great, but okay. 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3249995070

The world, though stunning, lacks the interactivity and dynamic events found in other open-world games like The Witcher 3 or Red Dead Redemption 2. There are few surprises, and after a while, exploration can feel monotonous. The constant need to follow the wind to the next objective, while initially unique, quickly becomes another repetitive mechanic.

The sound design is pretty good. The traditional Japanese instruments and melodies enhance the atmosphere. The ambient sounds, like the rustling leaves and flowing water, make the world feel more immersive. The combat sounds, from the clash of swords to the arrows flying, are crisp and impactful.

Ghost of Tsushima is the highly polished combat version of Assassin's Creed plus stunning nature visuals. But it's held back by ordinary game design with repetitive open-world activities, side quests, and generic storytelling. Do I think it's overrated? Absolutely, but It's a fun time, recommended on a sale.

[b]As a longtime fan of samurai tales and open-world adventures, Ghost of Tsushima has been one of my most anticipated games. The moment it was announced for PC, I knew I had to experience it, no matter the hurdles. Unfortunately, the game was region-blocked in many countries, and I even went as far as changing my country just to purchase it. [h1]A Breathtaking Journey Through Feudal Japan[/h1]
[b]Set during the Mongol invasion of Tsushima in 1274, the game follows Jin Sakai, a samurai torn between honor and survival, as he defends his homeland from an overwhelming enemy. From the very first scene, Ghost of Tsushima captivates with its stunning visuals, epic narrative, and atmospheric soundtrack. The game brings feudal Japan to life with unparalleled beauty, from serene forests and golden fields to violent battlefields and peaceful shrines.[/b]

[h1]Engaging Narrative and Character Development[/h1]
[b]The story of Jin Sakai is one of honor, sacrifice, and personal struggle. As Jin transitions from a traditional samurai to the stealthy "Ghost," his journey explores themes of loyalty, morality, and what it truly means to protect one’s people. The supporting cast is equally memorable, with characters like Lady Masako, Yuna, and Sensei Ishikawa each bringing emotional depth and compelling subplots.
The narrative strikes a perfect balance between personal storytelling and epic historical drama, keeping you engaged from start to finish.[/b]

[h1]Fluid Combat and Playstyle Freedom[/h1]
[b]The combat in Ghost of Tsushima is nothing short of spectacular. Whether you prefer the honorable approach of facing enemies head-on with your katana or the stealthier path of the Ghost, the game offers fluid, satisfying mechanics for both.
The samurai duels are cinematic and thrilling, requiring precision and patience, while the stealth mechanics allow you to creatively outsmart your foes. Coupled with Jin’s customizable gear, skills, and stances, the gameplay remains fresh and exciting throughout the adventure.[/b]

[h1]Exploration: A Living Work of Art[/h1]
[b]Few games make exploration feel as rewarding as Ghost of Tsushima. Instead of overwhelming the player with cluttered HUDs or waypoints, the game uses natural elements like wind, birds, and foxes to guide you, creating an immersive experience that encourages curiosity.
From uncovering hidden shrines to composing haikus at scenic locations, every moment of exploration feels meaningful. The island of Tsushima itself is a character, and its beauty is a constant source of awe.[/b]

[h1]Director's Cut: Iki Island and Beyond[/h1]
[b]The Director's Cut adds the Iki Island expansion, which deepens the narrative and explores Jin’s past. Iki Island offers new gameplay mechanics, unique enemies, and stunning landscapes that complement the main game. It’s a fantastic addition that elevates an already outstanding experience.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]

[*]Engaging combat: A perfect blend of samurai precision and stealth tactics.
[*]Immersive exploration: Natural guidance systems make exploration intuitive and rewarding.

First off, this is possibly the most breathtaking game that I've ever played. The world is made more immersive by the lack of UI and the use of its unique wind mechanic as its navigation system. However, the game does suffer from the repetitiveness of its map activities like most open-world games do. But what Ghost of Tsushima does really well in this aspect compared to others is that they actually offer great rewards in the form of permanent buffs e.g. maximum health boost, resolve increase & new skills. After spending 65 hours with Ghost of Tsushima, I can confidently say it's one of the best open-world action games I've played. While it didn't surpass Red Dead Redemption 2 as my favorite narrative-driven game, it delivered one of the most consistently enjoyable gameplay experiences I've had in years.

The combat is easily the game's greatest strength. Every encounter feels rewarding because of how many options the game gives you. Whether I was clearing camps with my bow, sneaking through enemy lines with assassinations, engaging in fast-paced sword duels, or relying on Ghost Weapons when things got overwhelming, combat never felt repetitive. The stance system constantly encouraged me to adapt instead of relying on a single strategy, making every fight feel satisfying from beginning to end.

Progression is another highlight. Unlocking new techniques, armor sets, charms, and Ghost Weapons always felt meaningful, and I enjoyed experimenting with different builds depending on my playstyle. Rather than pushing players toward a single "best" setup, Ghost of Tsushima gives you the freedom to create your own approach to combat, which made every upgrade feel rewarding.

Visually, the game is breathtaking. Its art direction is phenomenal, with beautiful landscapes, vibrant colors, and cinematic presentation that constantly made me stop and appreciate the world. Combined with its soundtrack and sound design, Ghost of Tsushima creates an atmosphere that's both immersive and memorable.

The story is one I genuinely enjoyed. Jin Sakai's journey and the conflict between honor and survival were compelling, but when I compare it to Red Dead Redemption 2, I still think RDR2 delivers the stronger narrative and more emotionally impactful character writing. Ghost of Tsushima tells a great story—it just didn't leave the same lasting impression on me that Red Dead Redemption 2 did.

That said, I don't think it's fair to simply say Ghost of Tsushima has "better gameplay" than Red Dead Redemption 2. They're trying to accomplish different things. Red Dead Redemption 2 excels at immersion, realism, and weighty gunplay, while Ghost of Tsushima focuses on fast, fluid, and highly responsive melee combat. I preferred Ghost of Tsushima's sword combat and gameplay loop, but Red Dead Redemption 2 still has some of the best gunplay and world interaction in gaming.

Ultimately, Ghost of Tsushima succeeds because it understands what makes an action game fun. Every mechanic, from combat to exploration and progression, works together seamlessly to create an experience that's consistently engaging. It's one of those rare games where clearing "just one more camp" somehow turns into another hour of gameplay.

Ghost of Tsushima may not have surpassed Red Dead Redemption 2 as my favorite story-driven game, but it's easily one of the best action games I've ever played. If Red Dead Redemption 2 set the standard for storytelling and immersion, Ghost of Tsushima set one of the highest standards for melee combat and player-driven gameplay.

Ghost of Tsushima is an exceptional work of art, featuring what I consider the most impressive title card drop in the history of creative works—this moment signaled the beginning of a truly memorable adventure.

The graphics, swordplay, and music represent the pinnacle of excellence—visuals that are breathtakingly detailed, a combat system that is incredibly satisfying, and a score that perfectly complements the game's atmosphere. [h1]Ghost of Tsushima Review[/h1]

[i]This review contains spoilers.[/i]

There are games that eventually become modern classics. Whether you personally enjoy them or not, they're experiences that I believe everyone should try at least once. Games like Red Dead Redemption 2, Undertale, Hollow Knight, Hades, Disco Elysium, and The Witcher 3 come to mind. You might end up loving them or hating them, and you'll almost always come away appreciating something about them. In my opinion, Ghost of Tsushima belongs in that category.

I'm generally not a huge fan of Japanese settings, samurai stories, or feudal era aesthetics. Yet despite that, I couldn't help but appreciate everything this game made me feel and experience.

Normally, I finish a game within a few weeks, maybe a month at most. Ghost of Tsushima took me almost six months to complete and earn every achievement. Not because it was difficult. I simply couldn't bring myself to play it continuously. The story and gameplay never hooked me enough to binge through it. I even tried rushing it at one point, but that only made the experience worse. Eventually, I realized this wasn't the kind of game that wanted to be rushed, so I slowed down and played it the way I felt it deserved to be played exploring every region, completing every side activity, collecting everything I could find, and simply taking in the world.

I also went into the game completely blind after a friend recommended it to me. We usually have very similar tastes, so I trusted their suggestion. For some reason, I genuinely expected Ghost of Tsushima to have demons, monsters, or some kind of supernatural enemies. Instead, I found myself fighting human beings in a grounded historical setting, which made me laugh at just how wrong my expectations were. Since it was originally a PS4 title, I also went in with fairly moderate expectations. I couldn't have been more wrong.

The environmental design completely blew me away. I genuinely lost count of how many times I stopped what I was doing just to enter Photo Mode and admire the scenery. Every region feels handcrafted, and despite spending months exploring the island, I never got tired of looking at it.

Usually, when I play a game, I imagine myself as the main character. Their choices become my choices. Ghost of Tsushima was different. I never felt like I was Jin Sakai. Instead, I felt like I was witnessing his journey unfold. The voice acting, facial expressions, motion capture, and cinematic presentation are phenomenal. Every loss, sacrifice, moment of guilt, and the burden he carried for the people of Tsushima felt believable. I don't think another game has made me empathize with a protagonist in quite the same way.

One aspect that surprised me the most was how naturally the game challenged both Jin's beliefs and my own. Jin was raised as a samurai. Honour, discipline, and tradition are woven into every part of his identity. Coincidentally, I'm also the kind of player who dislikes stealth, assassinations, or deceptive tactics whenever I have the option, so our philosophies aligned almost perfectly. For almost the entire first half of the game,I wore the Traveler's Attire because I didn't want to miss any collectibles, while every encounter was approached the samurai way. No assassinations. No dirty tricks. Just honourable combat. Act I went exactly how I wanted it to.

Then Act II slowly started changing both Jin and me. There came a point where I realized honour alone simply wasn't enough anymore. The samurai code couldn't solve every problem, and I think that's exactly what the developers wanted the player to feel. Every assassination became a little easier to justify, and every dirty trick became another necessary evil.

Then Act III began, and my horse died.
Strangely enough, that moment hurt. It felt like I had lost a companion rather than just another game mechanic. From that point onward, my admiration for the samurai way slowly faded. The more I listened to their dialogue, understood their ideals, and watched the decisions they made, the more they felt like nobles obsessed with preserving honour and reputation even if innocent people had to suffer for it.

It made me question everything.

[i]Is this really justice? Is this really what the samurai stood for?[/i]

With the samurai code becoming an actual disadvantage against the Mongol invasion, Jin was forced to abandon many of the ideals he had grown up believing in. Poison. Assassinations. Ambushes. Deception. Rallying ordinary people to fight beside him. He used whatever means were necessary simply to give Tsushima a chance to survive.
What I appreciate most is that the game never portrays Jin as perfect. He makes mistakes. His decisions have consequences. He regrets some of them and tries to make things right. He's simply human. Ironically, I think it's that humanity, rather than his title as a samurai, that ultimately allows him to become the Ghost.

The Mongols are portrayed exceptionally well. They're brutal enough to make you despise them, especially when you witness what they do to ordinary villagers. At the same time, it's hard not to admire how intelligent and adaptable they are. They studied the samurai, understood their code, discovered its weaknesses, and weaponized those weaknesses against them. One of my favourite examples is how they eventually begin using Jin's own poison against the people of Tsushima. That single decision perfectly demonstrates one of the game's central themes: every action has consequences, even when your intentions are good.
Nothing remains black and white anymore.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Iki Island[/h2]

Iki Island was a really interesting post game experience. It explores Jin's childhood, the trauma surrounding his father's death, and the guilt he carried from being unable to save him. What I initially expected to be a simple expansion but ended up adding a surprising amount of depth to Jin as a character.

The DLC also shows that the samurai weren't always as honourable as they claimed to be. They destroyed villages, tore families apart, and justified it all in the name of bringing a lawless island under samurai rule. It gives you a much deeper understanding of Jin's internal conflict and why he struggles so much with honour throughout the main story.

It also features some incredible set pieces. Charging into battle alongside an army had my adrenaline pumping, and those moments ended up being some of my favourites in the entire game.

[hr][/hr]
[h2]Legends Mode[/h2]

Ironically, Legends Mode was much closer to what I originally imagined Ghost of Tsushima would be. It's brutal, supernatural, and brings unique abilities. It takes the combat from the base game and expands upon it with different classes and MMO style loot progression that steadily improves your character over time. The mode itself is well made and a lot of fun.

Unfortunately, it also became my least favourite part of earning every achievement. The player population is fairly small now, which means many modes are difficult to find matches for. I often found myself replaying the same maps because matchmaking for higher difficulties took a very long time.

Unlocking the raid, finding a team through Discord, and grinding for all the multiplayer achievements eventually started feeling more like a chore than something I wanted to do. Honestly, I think the achievement design is one of the game's weakest aspects. I completely understand requiring achievements for the base game and Iki Island. Locking 100% completion behind a separate multiplayer mode that many players will never touch, however, feels unnecessary.

[hr][/hr]
Overall, Ghost of Tsushima is an experience I'd recommend everyone try at least once. It wasn't a game made for someone like me, yet six months later, I walked away appreciating it.

This game is almost perfection everything from the ultra-realistic renderings of Japan to the combat to the acting is incredible. I also love the story and Jin's conflicted nature about the rogue element of his combat style.

Historically, they were such an existential threat that warring provinces in Eastern Europe called a truce with each other and banded together to drive them back to Asia.

People have complained about this game's repetitiveness. Yes, sometimes the combat is somewhat repetitive, but to me it's the GOOD kind of repetitive. I'm not annoyed by it.

The game feels alive — from the smallest detail in a bamboo forest to the weight of every decision Jin makes. The combat is tight and satisfying, the visuals breathtaking, and the atmosphere feels like art in motion.

I’ve played a lot of open-world games, but few have moved me like this one. Even compared to newer titles like Assassin’s Creed Shadows, Ghost of Tsushima still holds a special place — it’s not just beautiful, it’s meaningful.

Ghost of Tsushima: The PC Port We Dreamed Of

I’m giving this a thumbs up with 6 hrs playtime, but I did play it on PS5 
and I couldn’t wait to experience it again on PC with my OLED 240Hz monitor.

This game is literally a moving painting where every duel feels like it belongs on the big screen. The story is rich, combat is sharp. Ghost of Tsushima is one of those rare games that makes you stop mid-ride just to admire the world around you.

On PC, it’s even better.
Frame Generation runs flawlessly no ghosting, no artifacts. Frametimes are the smoothest I’ve experienced across any FG title so far. Rock-solid consistency, no stutter, just steady 5–7ms. The frametime graph? Flat as glass. Sucker Punch and Nixxes delivered a gold-standard port.

Gameplay is incredible, Ubisoft could never. Combat is cinematic but precise, letting you flow between stances, counters, and deadly finishing moves. The story is heartfelt, layered with themes of honor, loss, and sacrifice. Side quests aren’t filler they enrich the world. And every duel feels like it belongs in a samurai film.

What really sets it apart is the guiding wind. No minimap. No clutter. Just nature pulling you forward. It’s one of the most immersive mechanics I’ve ever experienced. Instead of staring at waypoints, I’m in the world, watching leaves blow, following birds, feeling Tsushima itself guide me. The HUD is minimal by design, letting the environment tell the story. Every sound, every gust, every flick of a fox’s tail draws you deeper in.

This game is so beautiful that Photo Mode will eat hours of your life and you’ll become The Ghost of Instagram.

and to be real with you, the only downside is there is no target lock on keyboard and mouse (it’s there for controller users). That’s it.

Combat: Flows like poetry, cuts like steel.
Visuals: Cinematic, alive, unforgettable — HDR makes it shine.
Photo Mode: Ghost of Instagram.
Port Quality: Gold standard — no stutter, no shader drama, just smooth steel and beauty.

If you loved it on PlayStation, this PC version is the definitive way to experience Tsushima. If you’re new, prepare for one of the most beautiful and immersive journeys gaming has to offer.
